title: Workflow basics: Mark Adamus’s minimal-tool, clone-painting landscape post-processing
summary: In this tutorial, Mark Adamus outlines his core approach to post-processing landscape images, advocating a ‘less is more’ philosophy and a focused toolset. He explains his philosophy of predicting results before acting, then demonstrates a streamlined RAW/ACR workflow followed by Photoshop-based refinement. A central feature is his clone-painting workflow (which he notes he invented in 2005) used to blend textures and colors non-destructively, supplemented by focus stacking, sky-water composites, and atmospheric adjustments. The video covers practical steps—from dynamic-range adjustments in RAW, through Bridge/Camera Raw syncing, to Photoshop techniques like auto-align/auto-blend for focus stacks, perspective and puppet warps, and diffusion-based luminosity—culminating in a guided emphasis on lighting direction, color balance, and the viewer’s eye path. Throughout, Adamus emphasizes field discipline, non-destructive editing, and the importance of creating cohesive transitions rather than heavy-handed, pixel-level alterations.

sections.title: Clone painting system & non-destructive composite work

sections.description: Details the central clone-painting workflow, its history in Adamus’s practice, and how it’s used to blend sky, water and foreground while maintaining a cohesive look. Covers non-destructive layering, distillation of edits via history brush, and enhancements like diffusion and luminosity passes.

sections.title: Artistic philosophy & final guidance
concepts: less is more; mastery of a small toolset
directional light guiding the viewer’s eye
sections.description: Concludes with high-level guidance on maintaining a painterly feel, and the importance of transitions and directional lighting to guide the viewer’s gaze.
